questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain how a solution of a system is confirmed
questions.stem: Note 2004 asks how a translator should confirm that a triple of values is the solution of a system of three equations.

answer.exemplar: A candidate triple is confirmed by substitution: each value is placed into each equation in turn and the two sides are compared. For the system x plus y plus z equals 12, x minus y equals 2, and y plus z equals 7, the triple 5, 3, 4 gives 12 on the first, 2 on the second, and 7 on the third, so all three hold and the triple is the solution. Checking only the equation that was used last is the usual way a wrong triple survives.

questions.explanation: Substitution is the test because the system is a set of claims about the same three numbers, and a claim that fails once is simply false. Checking each equation removes the chance of a lucky agreement in one place.
questions.hint: Substitute the values back into every equation.

questions.topic: Word problem solved by a system
questions.learningObjective: explain how to check a word problem solution
questions.stem: Note 2011 asks for a way of checking a solution to a word problem that was built from a system of two equations.

answer.exemplar: A word problem solution is checked by putting the values back into the words of the problem, not only into the algebra. If the two projects each have 15 pages, the billing rule of a fixed 45 dollars plus 12 dollars per page gives 225 dollars for one project, so the pair comes to 450 dollars, which is the total in the note. The check works because the words, the equations, and the arithmetic all agree, and a mismatch points to a mistake in the model rather than in the arithmetic.

questions.explanation: The words of the problem are the source of the equations, so checking against them catches a badly built model that algebra alone will miss. Recomputing the totals shows which part went wrong.
questions.hint: Recompute the total from the words of the problem.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Dividing by a possibly zero expression
questions.learningObjective: explain how to record a restriction when dividing by an expression
questions.stem: Note 2016 asks how a translator should record the restriction that comes from dividing by an expression in an equation.

answer.exemplar: The restriction has to be written down at the moment the division is made, because it is a condition on the original equation rather than on the rearranged one. In the equation x plus 5 over x minus 2 equals 3, the divisor requires x not equal to 2, and that is true of every solution of the original equation, while the rearranged equation x plus 5 equals 3x minus 6 does not mention it. Recording the restriction keeps the check on the answer honest.

questions.explanation: The rearranged equation silently forgets the value the division removed, so the restriction must travel with the work. Written beside the solution, it shows which answer to discard.
questions.hint: Write the forbidden value down before you divide.

questions.stem: Note 2022 asks how the solution set of a linear inequality should be described in a translator's notes.

answer.exemplar: The solution set of a linear inequality is not a single number but a stretch of the number line, described by an endpoint and a direction. questions.learningObjective: explain why a negative divisor reverses an inequality
questions.stem: Note 2028 asks for an explanation of why dividing an inequality by a negative number reverses its direction.

answer.exemplar: Dividing by a negative number is the same as multiplying by one half of a negative number, and a negative multiplier turns a larger number into a smaller one, so the comparison has to be reversed. In -4x at least 12, the right side is positive, so x has to be negative, and after the division the bound is x at most minus 3. Keeping the direction would put positive values such as 0 into a set where they do not belong.

questions.explanation: The reversal is a fact about negative multipliers, and a quick substitution confirms it. Treating a negative divisor like a positive one produces bounds that admit values the inequality rejects.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain how a compound inequality is worked through
questions.stem: Note 2034 asks for an explanation of how a compound inequality should be worked through.

answer.exemplar: A chained inequality states two conditions that must hold at the same time, so it is worked in two steps that keep both bounds: add or subtract first, then divide or multiply, reversing the direction if the divisor is negative. For minus 2 less than 3x minus 1 at most 11, adding 1 gives minus 1 less than 3x at most 12, and dividing by 3 gives minus 1/3 less than x at most 4. Splitting the chain into two alternatives would describe a much larger set.

questions.explanation: Each operation has to be applied to the middle term while both ends travel with it, which keeps the two conditions intact. Splitting the chain loses that link and describes a set with two pieces.
questions.hint: Apply each operation to the middle and to both bounds.

questions.stem: Note 2040 asks for an explanation of why an absolute value equation can have two solutions.

answer.exemplar: The absolute value of a quantity is its distance from zero, so a statement that the distance equals 11 describes two points, one on each side of zero, which is why the equation 2x minus 7 equals 11 and 2x minus 7 equals minus 11 must both be solved. The two cases are 11 and minus 11 rather than 11 twice, because the inside can point either way. Reporting only the positive case silently discards a genuine solution.

questions.explanation: Two solutions are the normal case rather than a special trick, because the expression can be positive or negative while keeping the same magnitude. Splitting into the two cases fully solves the equation.
questions.hint: The quantity inside can point either way from zero.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain why substitution keeps the solutions of a pair
questions.stem: Note 2046 asks for an explanation of why substitution works when solving a pair of equations.

answer.exemplar: When one equation in a pair is already written as an expression for one variable, that expression can be substituted wherever that variable appears in the other equation, and the pair then becomes a single equation in one unknown. Here y equals 2x plus 1, so replacing y in y equals 5x minus 14 gives 2x plus 1 equals 5x minus 14, and solving gives x equals 5 and y equals 11. The pair is a solution only because both original equations accept it.

questions.explanation: Substitution replaces one equation with an equivalent statement, so the set of values satisfying the pair is unchanged. The values that satisfy the new equation are exactly the pairs that satisfy both originals.
questions.hint: Substitution replaces an equation with an equivalent one.

questions.learningObjective: explain why multiplying by the common denominator is safe
questions.stem: Note 2052 asks for an explanation of why multiplying an equation by the least common denominator preserves its solutions.

answer.exemplar: Clearing a fraction means multiplying every term of the equation by the same factor, and because both sides are multiplied by the same number the equality survives exactly. With 12 as the least common denominator of 3 and 4, the terms x over 3 and x over 4 become 4x and 3x, and the right side becomes 84, which is 7 times 12. The result describes exactly the same values of x as the original equation.

questions.explanation: The factor is applied to every term on both sides, so each fraction is rewritten in an equivalent form rather than changed in value. The cleared equation has the same solutions as the original.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Isolating the principal in a formula
questions.learningObjective: explain the steps used to isolate a letter in a formula
questions.stem: Note 2058 asks for an explanation of the steps used to isolate a letter in a formula.

answer.exemplar: To isolate a letter in a formula, work backwards through the operations that produced it, undoing each one on both sides and keeping every other symbol in place. Starting from S equals a plus nd, subtract a to get S minus a equals nd, then divide both sides by d to reach n equals S minus a over d. Dividing before removing the constant would divide a term that is not part of the product.

questions.explanation: The order of the undoing steps mirrors the order in which the formula was built, and every step is applied to the whole equation. Stopping early leaves the target letter attached to a constant or a product.
questions.hint: Undo the last operation first and keep the other symbols.
